title: Smallest Convex Hulls of Polygons
abstract: We study the problem of minimizing the area of the convex hull of k polygons with a total of n vertices in the plane, under translations and rigid motions for any fixed k ≥ 3. For any ε ∈ (0, 1), we give (1 + ε)-approximation algorithms running in O(ε^{-1/2} log n + ε^{1/2 - k}) time for translations, and in O(ε^{-1/2} log n + ε^{3/2 - 2k}) time for rigid motions. We also consider minimizing the perimeter of the convex hull under translations and obtain a (1 + ε)-approximation algorithm running in O(ε^{-1/2} log n + ε^{1/2 - k}log^{k-1}(1/ε)) time. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first results of this kind for k ≥ 3 polygons. Furthermore, for the special case of two polygons with n₀ and n₁ vertices (n₀ ≥ n₁), respectively, we give an O(n₀+n₁log²(n₀+n₁))-time algorithm for the minimum-perimeter problem. This significantly improves upon the best-known O((n₀+n₁)log²(n₀+n₁)) bound by eliminating the logarithmic overhead associated with the larger input size n₀.

      Abstract
We study the problem of minimizing the area of the convex hull of k polygons with a total of n
vertices in the plane, under translations and rigid motions for any fixed k ≥ 3. For any ε ∈ (0, 1),
we give (1 + ε)-approximation algorithms running in O(ε−1/2 log n + ε1/2−k ) time for translations,
and in O(ε−1/2 log n + ε3/2−2k ) time for rigid motions. We also consider minimizing the perimeter
of the convex hull under translations and obtain a (1 + ε)-approximation algorithm running in
O(ε−1/2 log n + ε1/2−k logk−1 (1/ε)) time. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first results
of this kind for k ≥ 3 polygons. Furthermore, for the special case of two polygons with n0 and n1
vertices (n0 ≥ n1 ), respectively, we give an O(n0 + n1 log2 (n0 + n1 ))-time algorithm for the minimum-
perimeter problem. This significantly improves upon the best-known O((n0 + n1 ) log2 (n0 + n1 ))
bound by eliminating the logarithmic overhead associated with the larger input size n0 .

 1      Introduction
We study the problem of minimizing the area of the convex hull of k polygons for any fixed
integer k ≥ 3 in the plane under translations and rigid motions. The translation problem
can be formulated as follows: Given k polygons C0 , . . . , Ck−1 with a total of n vertices in
the plane, determine a translation vector ti ∈ R2 for each polygon Ci such that the area of
                     S
the convex hull conv( (Ci + ti )) is minimized. The rigid motion problem allows reorienting
each input polygon. Observe that the target area remains unchanged when each polygon,
not necessarily convex, is replaced by its convex hull in linear time. Thus, we assume that
the input polygons are convex.
    Convex hull minimization has broad applications in shape analysis and packing; it
naturally arises when designing a smallest container that accommodates multiple objects
under allowed motions. Motivated by such settings, we study minimizing the area (and also
the perimeter) of the convex hull of multiple polygons under translations and rigid motions.
    Related problems such as overlap maximization, bundling, and packing have been studied
extensively under translations and rigid motions in the plane and higher dimensions (e.g., [16,
12, 15, 17, 11, 18, 8, 7]). For two convex polygons, near-linear or expected-linear-time

       1.1    Our results
       In this paper, we investigate the optimization of the convex hull area for a set of k convex
       polygons C0 , . . . , Ck−1 with n vertices in total in the plane, under translations and rigid
                                                                                   S
       motions for any fixed k ≥ 3. We show that the area function of conv( (Ci + ti )) is not
       convex in the translation space R2k−2 ; it may even fail to be convex along many lines or
       low-dimensional flats. We characterize structural changes in the convex hull via event surfaces,
       bound their number by O(n), and obtain an exact translation algorithm running in O(nη )
       time, where η = max{5, 4k − 8 + δ} for any fixed δ > 0.
           Our core structural contribution reveals a hidden convexity in the translation space.
       While the area function is generally non-convex in R2k−2 , we establish that it becomes
       strictly convex when restricted to any cleverly chosen (k − 1)-dimensional affine subspaces.
       Moreover, we rigorously prove that k − 1 is the maximum possible dimension of an affine
       subspace of R2k−2 on which the area function is convex. This structural breakthrough is
       the key that reduces our effective search space from dimension 2k − 2 to k − 1, enabling our
       highly efficient (1 + ε)-approximation algorithms, running in O(ε−1/2 log n + ε1/2−k ) time
       for translations and O(ε−1/2 log n + ε3/2−2k ) time for rigid motions for any ε ∈ (0, 1).
           To the best of our knowledge, these are the first algorithms for k ≥ 3 polygons. Our
       approximation algorithms are significantly more efficient than the exact algorithm, as they
       identify translations in a (k − 1)-dimensional space. Furthermore, they are simple. The
       translation algorithm computes an optimal translation for the k convex polygons in a (k − 1)-
       dimensional space by constructing a cutting and finding the (k − 1)-flat containing the
       optimal translation recursively. The algorithm for rigid motion samples orientations of each
       polygon and determines the approximate translations for each orientation of each polygon
       using the translation algorithm.

    We identify an affine subspace of the translation space in which Υ(t) is convex and
piecewise linear. This subspace is referred to as the (t0 , a)-translation space T(t0 , a) with
a fixed unit vector t0 ∈ R2 and a fixed vector a ∈ R2k−2 . We show that T(t0 , a) has the
maximum dimension, k − 1, in which Υ(t) is convex. In T(t0 , a), each event surface is a
hyperplane.
    We design a linear-time algorithm to compute a translation t∗0 ∈ T(t0 , a) that satisfies
Υ(t∗0 ) ≤ Υ(t) for all t ∈ T(t0 , a). Let △ be an m-dimensional simplex with m ≤ k − 1 in
T(t0 , a). Let t△ be a translation in △ satisfying Υ(t△ ) ≤ Υ(t) for all t ∈ △. The algorithm
employs a procedure for computing an m-dimensional simplex △∗ ⊆ △ such that t△ ∈ △∗
and no event hyperplane intersects the interior of △∗ . Furthermore, the algorithm utilizes
an oracle that determines the relative position of t△ to an (m − 1)-flat intersecting △.
    The procedure operates as follows. It constructs a (1/2)-cutting of (m − 1)-dimensional
flats, each containing the intersection of △ and an event hyperplane. It obtains the cell
C△ containing t△ by executing the oracle with (m − 1)-dimensional faces of the cutting.
Subsequently, it triangulates C△ , executes the oracle with (m − 1)-dimensional faces of the
triangulation, and identifies an m-dimensional simplex containing t△ . It repeats this process
with the simplex and the event hyperplanes intersecting the simplex recursively until no
event hyperplane intersects the interior of the resulting simplex. Finally, it computes △∗ .
    The oracle works as follows. Assume that we have Υ(c) and a normalized directional
derivative at each vertex c of △. Given an (m − 1)-dimensional flat F , the oracle computes
an (m − 2)-dimensional simplex △′ that contains an optimal translation restricted to △ ∩ F
in time linear in the number of event hyperplanes intersecting △. Next, it computes a
normalized directional derivative at each vertex v of △′ . This is done by progressively
updating the derivative from a vertex c of △ along the segment connecting c and v, at each
intersection with the event hyperplanes. This process takes time linear in the number of
event hyperplanes intersecting the segment. We can determine the relative position of t△
with respect to F in the same asymptotic time bound for computing a minimum value of
Υ(t) in △ ∩ F . Then, the algorithm updates the derivatives at v by changing their directions
such that they point toward the interior of △′ . Similarly, it computes Υ(v) in time linear in
the number of event hyperplanes containing v.
    For N event hyperplanes intersecting an m-dimensional simplex, let T (N, m) and To (N, m)
denote the times for the procedure and the oracle, respectively. Then, T (N, m) = O(N ) +
O(To (N, m)) + T (⌊N/2⌋, m) and To (N, m) = O(N ) + T (N, m − 1). We show that T (N, m) =
O(N ) and To (N, m) = O(N ).
    Using the linear-time algorithm in the preceding paragraphs, we devise a (1 + ε)-
approximation algorithm. We assume that C0 has the longest diameter among all input
polygons and the segment connecting a diametral pair is horizontal. The algorithm constructs
O(1/ε) horizontal lines and computes a translation for each C ∈ C \ {C0 } such that the
topmost vertex of C ∈ C \ {C0 } is positioned on one of the horizontal lines. It enumerates
O(1/εk−1 ) distinct placements for the k − 1 topmost vertices over the horizontal lines, and
for each placement, computes an optimal translation t of the k − 1 polygons along their
corresponding lines using the linear-time algorithm in the preceding paragraphs. Thus, in
O(n/εk−1 ) time, the algorithm computes a translation tapx with Υ(tapx ) ≤ Υ(t) for all such
optimal translations t. We show that Υ(tapx ) ≤ (1 + ε)Υ(t∗ ). By approximating each input
polygon into a convex polygon with O(ε−1/2 ) vertices in the beginning of the algorithm, we
reduce the running time to O(ε−1/2 log n + ε1/2−k ).
    For the smallest convex hull problem under rigid motions, we generalize the method for
two polygons in [6]. We generate a set Si of O(1/ε) angles of Ci for each i = 1, 2, . . . , k − 1.
For each distinct rotation r = (θ1 , θ2 , . . . , θk−1 ) with θi ∈ Si , we compute a translation for

           The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces preliminaries. Section 3
       discusses the exact algorithm for computing the minimum-area convex hull for k polygons
       with k ≥ 3 under translations. In Section 4, we show that k − 1 is the maximum possible
       dimension of such a subspace. In Sections 5 and 6, we give (1 + ε)-approximation algorithms
       for the minimum-area convex hull under translations and rigid motions, respectively. Finally,
       in Appendix A, we consider the problem of minimizing the perimeter of the convex hull
       under translation and give an exact algorithm for two polygons, and a (1 + ε)-approximation
       algorithm for k polygons with k ≥ 3.

 3         Minimum-area convex hull under translations
We consider the problem of minimizing the area of the convex hull of k convex polygons
C0 , . . . , Ck−1 with n vertices in total in the plane under translations for any fixed k ≥ 3.
For ease of description, we assume that no input polygon has a vertical edge. This can be
achieved by a rotation if such an edge exists.

    Each event surface represents a set of translation vectors corresponding to the degeneracy
type. We can check whether a translation belongs to the set in O(1) time. We analyze
the number of event surfaces of type 1. For a fixed edge e of Ca + ta , Cb + tb touches the
supporting line of e from the same side at the same vertex (or edge) of Cb + tb . Thus, it is
bounded by the total number of edges of the polygons, which is O(n). For event surfaces
of type 2, since every polygon C ∈ C is convex, each vertex v of C has a unique interval of
orientations ϑ in [0, 2π) such that C is tangent to the line of angle ϑ mod π containing v.
For any two distinct vertices of C, their intervals are interior-disjoint. Thus, the intervals
of polygon vertices in C partition [0, 2π) into at most n intervals of orientations. For each
direction, each convex polygon has exactly one supporting vertex or edge; as direction varies,
the identity changes only O(n) times over all vertices, hence the number of event surfaces of
type 2 is O(n).
    Since T has dimension d = 2k − 2, applying the vertical decomposition for O(n) semi-
algebraic event surfaces in Rd yields a time complexity of O(n2d−4+δ ) = O(n4k−8+δ ) for any
fixed δ > 0 [14]. Evaluating Υ(t) for any fixed t in a cell takes O(n) time, which is O(n2k−1 )
for all O(n2k−2 ) cells. Thus, an optimal translation for Υ can be computed in O(nη ) time,
where η = max{4k − 8 + δ, 2k − 1} = max{4k − 8 + δ, 5} (2k − 1 ≥ 5 for k ≥ 3).
